DJI Matrice 30. Half the weight of the M300 on 16 in rotors and a 6S pack, against the M300's 21 in rotors and 12S. Its value here is SCALE: a model that only works at one size is not much of a model.

Validated against the published 36 min HOVER time, which DJI states separately from the 41 min flight time.

_published.battery: 2x TB30 in parallel, Li-ion 6S, 5880 mAh, 131.6 Wh, 685 g each

_inferred: Motor Kv and resistance, ESC parameters and airframe drag areas are NOT published. DJI names the motor (3511) and propeller (1671) but publishes no electrical parameters for either.
_calibration:
Nothing tuned — and it MISSES. The model gives 47.0 min hover against DJI's published 36, so it is 31% optimistic. This config is shipped BECAUSE it misses: it is the clearest evidence in the project of where this model stops being accurate.

What the numbers actually say, comparing overall hover efficiency (ideal momentum power divided by electrical power):
  M300, 21 in rotors: model 69.4%, real 69.2%  -- essentially exact
  M30,  16 in rotors: model 74.8%, real 57.3%  -- the model is far too kind

So the model has NO size dependence in its efficiency chain, while real hardware plainly does: the same design scaled down loses about 12 efficiency points. Smaller propellers run at lower Reynolds number, and smaller motors and ESCs are less efficient too. The model gets the large aircraft right almost exactly and carries that same efficiency down to half the size, where it does not hold.

This is NOT fixed here, deliberately. Two aircraft is not a scaling law, and fitting one to two points would be inventing a coefficient — the same mistake that made the propeller thrust fit 2x wrong earlier in this project. Correcting it needs bench data across a range of rotor sizes.

Practical consequence: trust this model least on small rotors. Below about 16 in, load a measured propeller table on the Propeller tab and the estimate is bypassed entirely.
